description:
We’re Team Matcha, a student team interested in space, technology, and creative ways to make science accessible. Our skills include web development, data visualization, interactive design, and turning ideas into working prototypes.

For Project Echo, we’re exploring how NASA climate data can become an experience people can hear, see, and interact with. We enjoy experimenting, learning from each other, and building something people can actually use.
summary:
ECHO is an interactive web experience that transforms NASA Earth Information Center visualizations and climate observations into sound. Users select authentic NASA imagery and explore soundscapes generated from its colors, positions, and pixel densities. They can also listen to two hidden climate periods, predict which was warmer, and reveal the NASA temperature measurements behind the tones.

ECHO addresses the Earth Information Jukebox challenge through dynamic, user-controlled sonification paired with source imagery and transparent explanations of the sound mappings. Its guided experience connects listening, prediction, and scientific evidence, supported by keyboard navigation, descriptive text, numerical tables, and adjustable playback.

By offering multiple ways to explore Earth science, ECHO aims to make climate information more engaging and accessible to students, educators, and blind or low-vision users. It encourages people to ask questions, investigate patterns, and build a closer understanding of our changing planet.
details:
What does the project do, and how does it work?

Project Echo transforms NASA climate data and imagery into an interactive listening experience. It uses NASA’s GISTEMP temperature observations to generate tones, with higher temperature anomalies producing higher pitches. Users listen to two hidden 30-year climate periods, predict which was warmer, and reveal the actual measurements. They can also explore annual observations from 1880–2025 and use an artistic instrument that converts colors and patterns in NASA imagery into sound.

What benefits does it have?

Project Echo gives people another way to explore climate patterns through sound, supported by charts, numerical data, and explanations. The listening test encourages active participation and curiosity. Keyboard controls, data tables, adjustable audio, and reduced-motion support give users several ways to navigate and understand the experience.

What is the intended impact?

We aim to make climate science more approachable for students, educators, and the public. By connecting NASA observations with an interactive experience, Project Echo encourages users to investigate long-term warming, ask questions, and connect what they hear with scientific evidence. Its guided classroom activity also supports discussion and exploration in educational settings.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did we use?

We developed Project Echo using React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, and the browser’s native Web Audio API. SVG charts display the observations, while browser canvas processing supports the image-to-sound instrument. NASA GISTEMP v4 provides the temperature data, and NASA’s Scientific Visualization Studio supplies the climate imagery. We used Vitest and Playwright for testing and Vercel for hosting. Codex assisted with development and documentation. The application runs in a web browser on a computer or phone, using speakers or headphones.

How is the project creative?

Project Echo combines climate science, sound, storytelling, and interactive discovery. Its blind listening test invites users to form a prediction before seeing the data. The image instrument adds an artistic way to explore NASA visualizations, while the sound laboratory lets users inspect how temperature measurements become musical pitch. Together, these experiences make the underlying data something users can listen to, question, and investigate.

What factors did the team consider?

We considered scientific accuracy, accessibility, usability, audio comfort, and transparency. Temperature observations use a consistent pitch mapping so comparisons remain meaningful. We explain the temperature baseline and distinguish the artistic interpretation of image pixels from the sonification of measured temperatures. We also considered mobile layouts, keyboard navigation, user-controlled playback, NASA attribution, and classroom use. The project is designed to support learning, with its educational impact still requiring evaluation through user testing.
